LVMH stock: AI rollout meets luxury-market caution
sum: LVMH is expanding practical artificial-intelligence applications across its luxury businesses after a November 3 meeting in Paris. The group said nearly 350 participants, including members of its Executive Committee and leaders from several Maisons, reviewed the next phase of the AI for ALL program.

The update gives investors a new look at how LVMH wants to turn AI pilots into business applications. At the Business of Tomorrow event, the group highlighted collection planning, sales support, customer relationships and operational optimization across its six business sectors.

LVMH said the program is intended to support employees while preserving human creativity, exceptional craftsmanship and personal client relationships. Stéphane Bianchi, Deputy General Manager, said each initiative should meet a real need, create value for the Maisons and have the potential to become a competitive advantage.

The company did not attach a new financial target to the initiative. For investors, the next test is whether individual Maisons convert the applications into measurable gains in service, sales support, customer engagement or operating efficiency.

A Reuters report published Friday placed luxury shares in a market shaped by uncertainty over the outlook for artificial-intelligence investments. The report said the broader luxury sector recorded a 2% session move, adding a wider market backdrop to LVMH's technology strategy.
LVMH stock traded at 404.45 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 18:11 CET on Friday, November 13, 2026.
Current market reports remain relevant as investors assess luxury demand, technology spending and the conversion of AI initiatives into operating benefits.

sum: LVMH spent the first week of November filing the paperwork that comes with being Europe's largest luxury group — and quietly pressing ahead with its artificial-intelligence agenda while brokers trimmed their expectations for the stock.

The Paris-based conglomerate submitted a notice to the French market regulator AMF on Tuesday covering share transactions carried out between 2 and 6 November. That filing followed an earlier disclosure, on 3 November, of buyback activity for the 26–30 October window. A separate mandatory notice, published on 5 November, set out the group's share capital as of 31 October: roughly 495 million shares, around 743 million gross voting rights and about 739 million net voting rights.

Away from the regulatory housekeeping, LVMH reported on 6 November that its "AI for ALL" programme is moving forward. Close to 350 participants turned up in Paris on 3 November for the third instalment of its "Business of Tomorrow" event, where attendees discussed how artificial intelligence is reshaping the group's operations. The gathering formed part of the ongoing AI initiative.

The group also used the week to extend a long-running tie-up with Central Saint Martins, renewing on 4 November a partnership centred on regenerative design. Both sides marked the new chapter of the collaboration at the London art and design school.

Louis Vuitton, the group's flagship label, featured in a separate Paris development. According to Le Monde, the city council approved a proposal under which the brand would fund and maintain improvements to streets running alongside its Champs-Élysées construction site. The reported plan covers upgrades worth an estimated EUR 2 million.

Investor attention, though, stayed fixed on demand. Wednesday's press coverage pointed to worries about a prolonged slump in appetite for high-end goods, with China drawing particular scrutiny. That anxiety was cited as the force behind the latest pressure on the luxury sector.

Morgan Stanley cut its price target for LVMH on Monday to EUR 415 from EUR 420, keeping an "Equal Weight" rating. The bank pointed to softer demand in China as well as weakening business activity in France and South Korea. Coverage of the day's luxury selloff tied the move to a tougher market outlook heading into year-end.

sum: LVMH used its platform at the China International Import Expo on Thursday to sketch out two very different brand moves in the world's second-largest economy: a first-ever Hennessy flagship boutique on Chinese soil and a Cruise 2028 runway moment for Dior, slated for Shanghai in 2027. The group already runs more than 1,400 stores across over 100 Chinese cities, so the announcements extend a footprint that is already deep rather than opening new territory.

The two projects share a market but not a shape — one is a retail build-out for the cognac house, the other a calendar date for the couture label. Both landed alongside the broader corporate messaging at the import fair.

Back in France, Louis Vuitton cleared a civic hurdle. According to Le Monde, the Paris city council approved the brand's proposal on 7 October to rework the Rue de Bassano and the Rue de Galilée, with the label footing the bill. The streets sit close to the planned mega-store on the Champs-Élysées, and the plan stirred debate over how much sway private companies should have over public space.

LVMH also turned its attention inward. Nearly 350 participants — among them members of the executive committee and the heads of the individual houses — gathered on 3 November for the third "Business of Tomorrow" event, according to company figures. The agenda centered on how artificial intelligence applies across the group's six business divisions. Separately, LVMH and Central Saint Martins extended their partnership aimed at advancing regenerative design.

Those brand and operational initiatives sit against a less encouraging financial backdrop. Berenberg issued a warning about a tough fourth quarter of 2026 for the luxury sector and rates LVMH at "Hold." The analysts, per Reuters, view China's demand weakness as structural, see continued downside risk to earnings estimates, and consider sector valuations stretched. Their advice to sell into rallies puts them at odds with a more upbeat HSBC.

The numbers behind the caution are concrete. Group revenue fell 1.6% to EUR 57,148 million in the first nine months of 2026, with currency effects shaving 3% off the top line. That split matters: exchange rates explain part of the drag, but the demand question stays at the heart of the investment case.

sum: LVMH is opening its ateliers to younger, more price-sensitive shoppers in a bid to rebuild desire after years of steep price hikes — a marketing pivot that lands just as analysts warn the demand backdrop is getting harder, not easier.

The group is following other luxury houses in staging experiences around its products, CNN reported, giving customers a closer look at craftsmanship and product development. The logic is straightforward: after aggressive price increases, established brands have to work harder to justify their value to more discerning buyers.

The scale of that repricing is striking. According to McKinsey, luxury prices rose by an average of 61% between 2019 and 2025. That puts the onus on LVMH to convince shoppers that workmanship, provenance and design add up to a fair exchange.

The outreach is aimed squarely at a cohort the industry can no longer take for granted. McKinsey data shows affluent newcomers and occasional luxury buyers account for roughly half of all luxury market sales. At the same time, 66% of US luxury customers consider challenger brands more exclusive than established names — a statistic that cuts to the heart of LVMH's dual challenge: affordability on one side, brand appeal on the other.
Craft demonstrations can explain a price tag. Whether they translate into purchases is another matter, and that is where the investment case ultimately rests.

The urgency is visible in the latest trading figures. LVMH posted revenue of EUR 18.504 billion in the third quarter of 2026, with organic growth of 1%. Beneath that headline, performance diverges sharply.

Fashion and leather goods — the group's largest engine — contracted 5% in the quarter. Watches and jewellery, by contrast, grew 8% organically over the first nine months of 2026, a sign that pockets of resilience remain.

It operates through the following segments: Wines and Spirits, Fashion and Leather Goods, Perfumes and Cosmetics, Watches and Jewelry, Selective Retailing, and Other and Holding Companies. The Wines and Spirits segment is involved in the production and sale of champagne wines and sparkling wines, as well as distribution of vodka and white liquor. The Fashion and Leather Goods segment offers luggage items, bags, accessories, shoes, and clothes. The Perfumes and Cosmetics segment distributes make-up, perfume, and skin care products. The Watches and Jewelry segment manufactures luxury watches and accessories for men and women. The Selective Retailing segment is organized to promote an environment that is appropriate to the image and status of the luxury brands. The Other and Holding Companies segment pertains to the media division, which publishes newspapers and magazines, manages business and financial websites, and holds radio stations. The company was founded by Bernard Arnault on January 13, 1923 and is headquartered in Paris, France.

sum: LVMH shares have now risen for four consecutive trading sessions, with the advance attributed in media reports to a recovery in European equity indices and a sector-wide rally in luxury names rather than to any fresh company-specific announcement. Over the past seven sessions the stock has gained 7.0%, though it gave back 0.6% on Friday.

The broader market backdrop has done the heavy lifting during the rebound, which media reports have also linked to optimism surrounding the US midterm election results. Beneath that headline move, however, the group's recent disclosures sketch a more mixed picture — spanning share buyback filings, an artificial intelligence push, a creative appointment and a fashion division still under pressure.

On Tuesday, LVMH said it had filed its declaration on transactions in its own shares with the French financial regulator AMF, covering dealings between 26 and 30 October. The notice's text carried no aggregate totals for the transactions. The filing documents trades already carried out and contained no announcement of a new repurchase programme.

Separately, Le Monde reported that Louis Vuitton has secured the Paris city council's approval for street modifications around its planned megastore on the Champs-Élysées. The group's flagship brand intends to redesign the Rue de Bassano and the Rue Galilée at its own expense. The council gave the green light on 7 October, and the proposal has stirred debate over the influence private companies wield over public space.
Under the arrangement, Louis Vuitton is covering the cost of maintaining the planters, according to company statements, while the city is to submit the construction application itself.

Louis Vuitton has also created a new brand stewardship role. Hector Muelas took up the position of Chief Brand Creative Officer on 1 November. According to media reports, he is responsible for brand storytelling and reports to deputy chief executive Damien Bertrand.

The corporate news lands against a softer trading backdrop. On 12 October, LVMH reported organic revenue growth of 1% for the third quarter of 2026. In the fashion and leather goods division, however, revenue fell 5% on an organic basis, with the company pointing to a less dynamic environment in China.

sum: Jefferies has reiterated its hold rating on LVMH with a price target of 415 euros, even as analyst James Grzinic trimmed his 2027 estimates below consensus on the back of persistently unfavourable demand conditions. The endorsement of the valuation came without any softening in his view of the trading environment, which he still describes as difficult.

The stock had strung together four consecutive sessions of gains through Thursday, a run media reports chalked up to a short-term recovery in the luxury sector and broader industry sentiment rather than any fresh company-specific catalyst. That streak snapped on Friday, when the shares gave up 0.6%.

Attention is also turning to the French capital's pavements. According to Le Monde, Louis Vuitton has committed up to 2 million euros to redesign two Paris streets adjacent to its forthcoming flagship store on the Champs-Élysées. The arrangement, reported on Tuesday, has stirred debate over the private financing of public spaces and the sway that private backers can exert over how those spaces are shaped.

On the legal front, the investigating magistrate overseeing the French inquiry into Hermès shares was planning to summon Bernard Arnault, Le Monde reported on 30 October. Jean-Jacques Guiony, a member of LVMH's executive committee, has already been questioned — explicitly in the capacity of a witness. For Arnault, the newspaper reported only the judge's intention to call him, not any questioning that has taken place. LVMH declined to comment on the ongoing proceedings.

The shares were down 1.4% today, a decline media coverage attributed to a broad selloff on the Paris bourse led by retreating US technology stocks, with other luxury names also coming under pressure. No company-specific trigger for that move was identified.

Louis Vuitton, meanwhile, has confirmed the appointment of Hector Muelas to lead creative brand direction, a decision ratified on 23 October and effective from 1 November. In the newly created role of Chief Brand Creative Officer, he reports to deputy chief executive Damien Bertrand and takes charge of brand storytelling and campaigns.

LVMH Discloses 494.6 Million Shares as Zenith Weighs Swiss Job Cuts
sum: LVMH has laid out its capital structure as of 31 October, reporting 494,606,080 outstanding shares in a regulatory disclosure. The filing puts gross voting rights at 743,358,184 and net voting rights at 739,382,278 — three separate figures that describe different facets of the group's ownership base. The notice is a snapshot at a fixed date, not a signal of any new transaction.

That distinction matters, because the disclosure lands alongside two unrelated developments at the French luxury giant: a repositioning at its watch brand Zenith and a French judicial review of the group's historical Hermès stake.

Zenith confirmed on 23 October that it will pivot toward higher-end timepieces and lower production volumes. The LVMH-owned brand simultaneously opened an employee consultation on the plan. According to media reports, as many as half of its Swiss workforce could be affected by job cuts.

No final decision on redundancies is expected before the consultation closes on 12 November, meaning the potential staff reductions remain undecided. The strategic shift itself, by contrast, has already been confirmed by the brand.

French investigators are also examining LVMH's role in the acquisition of Hermès shares. As Le Monde reported on 30 October, the probe into the vanished shares of Hermès heir Nicolas Puech has shifted its focus to that question. The investigating magistrate reportedly plans to summon Bernard Arnault — a reported procedural step in an ongoing inquiry, not a finding of wrongdoing.

The judge has also questioned LVMH executive Jean-Jacques Guiony about the historical purchase of a 17% stake in Hermès, linked to Puech's missing shares. LVMH has said it will not comment on pending proceedings. The scrutiny concerns the group's past stake-building in a rival, not its own shares covered by today's disclosure — and the filing offers no answer to those legal questions.

LVMH shares slipped 1.2% yesterday. On the corporate calendar, the Zenith consultation wraps up on 12 November, and the group's Nona Source platform — which reuses luxury materials — holds a sale in Paris from 24 to 28 November, a part of the business distinct from the watch brand's overhaul.

sum: LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton reported mixed nine-month results for the period ended September 30, 2026, with group growth masking a deeper setback in its largest business. World Footwear reported the figures on November 4, citing the company statement and comments from Chief Financial Officer Cécile Cabanis.
LVMH stock real-time quote traded at 406.40 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 12:16 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 2026.

Revenue reached 57.1 billion euros in the first nine months, down 2% on a reported basis but up 2% organically from the same period a year earlier. Organic growth strips out currency and portfolio effects, making it the clearer indicator of underlying trading momentum in the company report.

Third-quarter organic revenue increased 1% year on year to 18.5 billion euros. The result showed that LVMH continued to benefit from the breadth of its portfolio, but regional trends diverged. Business activity remained positive in the United States, Europe and Japan, while China became more subdued.

Fashion and Leather Goods, the group's largest division, generated 26.4 billion euros in the first nine months. Reported revenue declined 4% and organic revenue fell 2% from the comparable period in 2025. The deterioration accelerated in the third quarter, when divisional revenue fell 5% after a 1% increase in the second quarter.

Cabanis said the quarter brought a more challenging Chinese consumer backdrop, with consumer sentiment deteriorating at the beginning of the period. She also identified the Middle East situation as an additional headwind. The comments point to a demand problem concentrated in an important market rather than a broad contraction across every LVMH business.

All other LVMH divisions reported growth in the third quarter, according to the report. That diversification offers some protection for group revenue, but Fashion and Leather Goods remains central to the investment case because Louis Vuitton and Dior give the division disproportionate influence over the group's growth profile and investor sentiment.

sum: Zerodha co-founder Nikhil Kamath has recalled an interesting exchange with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, revealing that the artificial intelligence pioneer had recommended luxury stocks Hermès and LVMH when asked which companies investors should consider buying.

However, the picks have reportedly lost around 50% of their value since then, prompting Kamath to question whether the productivity gains promised by artificial intelligence are translating into real economic benefits.
Kamath shared the anecdote during a recent episode of his podcast, WTF is AI?, where he was joined by a panel of technology experts to discuss the AI boom.
The conversation has since attracted attention on social media, with users debating Altman's investment thesis and the gap between expectations surrounding AI and the economic reality.
The exchange originally took place when Kamath interviewed Altman last year. Recalling the conversation, Kamath said he had asked the OpenAI chief which stocks he should buy.
According to Kamath's recollection, Altman's recommendation was based on the expectation that artificial intelligence would dramatically improve productivity.
The underlying argument was that as AI tools make individuals and businesses more productive, people would eventually have greater financial resources and disposable income.

items.t: LVMH Denies Puech Hermès Stake Interest as Zenith Weighs Swiss Cuts
sum: LVMH has flatly rejected a report that it wants to buy Nicolas Puech's stake in Hermès, pushing back on a Le Monde story published Friday that surfaced amid a judicial probe into shares belonging to the Hermès heir that have reportedly gone missing. The denial lands alongside a separate, unrelated disclosure: the luxury group's own share buybacks, detailed in a regulatory notice Tuesday covering repurchases made between October 19 and 23, with the stated purpose of cancelling the stock under a program approved on April 23.

The two threads — a criminal investigation touching LVMH's history with Hermès stock and a routine capital measure involving LVMH's own equity — concern entirely different matters and should not be conflated, the company's filings imply.

At the center of the Le Monde account is Jean-Jacques Guiony, an LVMH executive questioned as a voluntary witness by an investigating magistrate about the group's historical purchases of Hermès shares. The probe itself focuses on stock that Puech's former wealth manager is alleged to have sold. LVMH has denied any intention of taking over Puech's holding.

For investors, the gap between what is being investigated and what has actually been established matters. The report describes a witness interview and the company's position — nothing more. It does not demonstrate any unlawful acquisition by LVMH, nor does it assign the group responsibility for the missing shares. The rejection of takeover intent is likewise the company's own statement, not a court finding.

Away from the legal headlines, LVMH is reshaping its brands. At Louis Vuitton, Hector Muelas steps into the newly created role of Chief Brand Creative Officer today, taking charge of creative brand communications and campaigns and reporting to deputy CEO Damien Bertrand, according to media reports. The appointment was announced on October 23. It gives the brand's creative presentation its own leadership post — a decision about marketing and campaigns, not a signal of recovering demand or rising sales.
Zenith, the group's watchmaker, is charting a different course.

sum: Buffets were set up all around the grounds of this magnificent 19th-century hôtel particulier, which serves as the residence for American ambassadors in France, just a few steps from the Elysée Palace. Was it that rather kitsch orchestra accompanying "O Sole Mio" and other popular Italian songs sung by Andrea Bocelli, wearing a jacket and blue-tinted aviator glasses, in front of 2,000 guests in cocktail attire? Or perhaps, a little further away and protected by security officers, that small circle of leading industry executives and VIP guests greeting Charles Kushner, father of Jared Kushner – the son-in-law and business associate of Donald Trump? It felt like a scene straight out of the opening of Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather (1972).

Thousands of kilometers away, in Washington, on the eve of July 4, the US president was preparing to kick off the celebrations for the 250th anniversary of US independence. Meanwhile, in Paris, "the honorable Charles Kushner" – pardoned by Trump after being convicted of financial misconduct and subsequently appointed by him as ambassador to Paris – decided to mark the occasion by paying tribute to a Frenchman whose "commercial success is legendary": Bernard Arnault, the "guest of honor," whose name was printed in gold letters on the invitations.

One hour before most of the guests flooded into the embassy's sprawling gardens, a private party of the roughly 80 most generous guests had already gathered around Kushner and the LVMH chief executive. Alongside Arnault, accompanied by three of his sons – Antoine, Alexandre and Frédéric – were Patrick Pouyanné, the CEO of TotalEnergies, Alexandre Ricard, CEO of Pernod Ricard, and Slawomir Krupa and Jean-Laurent Bonnafé, the heads of Société Générale and BNP Paribas banks. All had contributed their share – at least €100,000 each, with the Arnault family contributing €3 million of the €9 million raised by the embassy – to fund the celebrations as well as the renovation of the splendid three-story building.

(Il Sole 24 Ore Radiocor) - Luxury under pressure as Milan Men’s Fashion Week draws to a close and the start of Paris Men’s Fashion Week approaches. Most stocks in the sector are on the decline, amid fears that rising oil prices and geopolitical tensions could end up undermining tourism, which has always been closely linked to the luxury business. Another concern is the prospect that the spread of artificial intelligence could affect the incomes of the middle class and, in the long term, reduce the consumer base for high-end brands. It is no coincidence that, in recent days, an interesting report by Bernstein has prompted a series of reflections on the repercussions that an increasingly ‘K-shaped’ society might have on the world of fashion: a scenario characterised by a rise in the number of low-income earners and the ultra-rich, alongside a gradual decline in the middle class.

In Milan, Brunello Cucinelli and Moncler are among the worst performers on the FTSE MIB, which is weak Salvatore Ferragamo. In Paris, however, caution is spreading to LVMH and Kering, whilst Hermès is faring even worse. Swiss firm Richemont and British firm Burberry are also down.

Shares are also trading on Essilorluxottica, which is also affected by uncertainties regarding the future of its largest shareholder, Delfin, which holds over 30% of the share capital. Indeed, the dispute between the Del Vecchio heirs continues, and the possibility is taking shape that the holding company itself might acquire the shares held by Luca and Paola Del Vecchio, who are keen to sell. This scenario has gained momentum following Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio’s decision to step back, announced in recent days in QN, due to difficulties in securing the financing needed to support the transaction.

European Luxury Stocks Surge on Proposed US-Iran Peace Deal
sum: Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.

European luxury equities experienced a massive valuation surge on Friday, June 12, following the publication of a proposed 14-point peace memorandum between the U.S. and Iran. The tentative diplomatic framework, which outlines the lifting of U.S. oil sanctions and the guaranteed reopening of the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, triggered an immediate risk-on rotation across continental trading floors.

Shares in high-end design houses LVMH, Kering, and Hermès skyrocketed by roughly 5%, leading a broader market rally that pushed the pan-European STOXX 600 index up 1.8% to reverse weeks of energy-driven stagflation fears.

The explosive rebound across luxury portfolios followed an official report from Iranian state media detailing a comprehensive diplomatic breakthrough with Washington. According to the leaked memorandum of understanding, Tehran has committed to fully restoring international shipping access through the narrow Strait of Hormuz within 30 days. In exchange, the U.S. will unwind its restrictive crude oil embargoes.

The economic relief was immediate. Prior to the announcement, the effective closure of the primary maritime channel had sent energy prices surging, fueling persistent inflation fears that forced the European Central Bank to implement hawkish interest-rate adjustments. While President Donald Trump later tempered the market enthusiasm via social media by stating that the accord was subject to the finalization of official documents, reports confirm that senior diplomats are on track to sign the treaty ahead of the upcoming Group of Seven leaders' summit.

The luxury sector emerged as the primary beneficiary of this geopolitical de-escalation. In Paris, LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE and Gucci owner Kering SA both jumped 5%, while ultra-premium leather goods titan Hermès International advanced nearly 5%. In Zurich, Cartier parent Richemont rose 3.4%.

Jay-Z Could Become Co-Owner of Rihanna’s Fenty Beauty
sum: *A potential blockbuster deal could soon unite two of entertainment’s biggest names under one beauty empire.

Jay-Z’s investment platform MarcyPen Capital Partners is reportedly the frontrunner to buy out luxury conglomerate LVMH’s share of Fenty Beauty, Beauty Independent reports. The stake in question represents half the company. Rihanna owns the other half and would continue steering the brand alongside whoever completes the purchase.

Jay-Z’s firm previously backed Savage X Fenty lingerie line during two separate fundraising rounds. MarcyPen came together in 2024 when Marcy Venture Partners merged with Pendulum Opportunities, and the combined entity now oversees roughly $1.1 billion in assets. Jay-Z built the firm alongside entertainment executive Jay Brown, entrepreneur D’Rita Robinson, and Robbie Robinson, who once advised President Barack Obama on financial matters.

LVMH quietly signaled its interest in exiting its Fenty Beauty position last October, bringing in Evercore to gauge buyer interest. The brand moved about $450 million in products during 2024, and analysts currently peg its total value somewhere between $1 billion and $2 billion.

Fenty Beauty’s cultural footprint, however, remains undeniable. When Rihanna debuted the line at Sephora in 2017, its 40-shade foundation range forced the entire beauty industry to rethink its approach to inclusivity. The brand has grown steadily since, moving into skincare, fragrance, and haircare before landing an exclusive body care line at Ulta Beauty last year.

items.t: Armani weighs splitting 15% stake among EssilorLuxottica, L’Oréal and LVMH – report
sum: Giorgio Armani SpA is considering selling a 15% minority stake in three 5% tranches to L'Oréal, LVMH and EssilorLuxottica, according to Italian publication la Repubblica.
The move is part of a succession plan tied to the will of founder Giorgio Armani, who passed away on 4 September 2025.
Armani CEO Giuseppe Marsocci is preparing a five-year business plan to be presented to investment banks that will help select advisers and potential investors from 9 September.

Under the will, a 15% stake must be sold within 12 to 18 months of its reading, with priority given to companies named by Armani: LVMH, EssilorLuxottica, L'Oréal, or another fashion or luxury group of similar standing.
Any choice would require the approval of Leo Dell'Orco, Armani's longtime partner and heir to a 40% holding in Giorgio Armani SpA.
The sale process has not formally started, but the group is expected to appoint at least two advisers, with Rothschild seen as a likely candidate.

Splitting the stake among the three named groups is said to be under review to preserve strategic flexibility while the company executes the founder's vision of a "democratic" luxury house spanning categories from EA7 and Emporio Armani to Armani Privé.

sum: Bernard Arnault’s annual salary as LVMH’s CEO has been revealed.
Arnault became the major shareholder of the luxury products group in 1989, taking on the role of Chair and CEO from the same date.
In addition, he serves as President of the Board of Directors of Groupe Arnault S.E., his family holding company.
Arnault’s annual gross fixed compensation for 2026 is €1.1m (€1,138,307) – the same amount as he was paid in 2025, according to a document shared by LVMH.

See how Arnault’s annual salary compares to Kenvue CEO Kirk Perry, Shiseido CEO Kentaro Fujiwara, L'Oréal CEO Nicolas Hieronimus, Coty Interim CEO Markus Strobel and Estée Lauder Companies CEO Stéphane de La Faverie.

Documentation from LVMH’s shareholder meeting on 23 April revealed that “compensation paid to the Chair and CEO also includes a variable annual component based on the achievement of financial (quantifiable), strategic and managerial (qualitative), and CSR and sustainability‑related (quantifiable and qualitative) targets”.

The financial (quantifiable) criteria relates to growth in the group’s revenue, profit from recurring operations and cash flow relative to the budget trajectory for the year in question, and isa said to account for 50% of total variable compensation for Arnault.

4 Takeaways From Luxury’s Q1 Earnings
sum: Luxury’s hopes for a slight first-quarter rebound have been set back, as conflict in the Middle East delivers a blow to performance.

“Q1 didn’t really change the sector’s outlook, and, if anything, it slowed down or pushed back the recovery story we had in mind,” Barclays head of European luxury goods research Carole Madjo says. “The market has lowered its Q2 estimates to factor in the impact of the Middle East conflict and the disrupted tourism environment. The sector’s downgrade cycle is still ongoing on the top line, and potentially on margins as well.”
HSBC anticipated a 5.5% increase in global luxury sales in Q1 2026. However, the average organic sales growth of LVMH, Kering, Hermès, Moncler, and Prada materialized at 4.2%.

“For most companies, momentum in China is improving every quarter. The big issue continues to be the drop in Chinese tourism,” TD Cowen analyst Oliver Chen says. “The US continues to be a resilient and attractive market, with a K-shaped economy — where the top end grows, but the lower end is seeing more pressure particularly as consumers watch gas prices. The strongest momentum comes from jewelry.”

While soft luxury brands have shown relative weakness, the jewelry “supercycle” continues. Sales at LVMH’s watches and jewelry division, Kering’s jewelry arm, and Hermès jewelry were up 7%, 22%, and almost 10%, respectively. This bodes well for Cartier owner Richemont, which will publish its annual earnings on May 22.

At LVMH’s annual general meeting on April 23, chair and CEO Bernard Arnault warned investors that the Middle East crisis “could turn into a global catastrophe with extremely serious and very negative economic consequences”. He added: “In which case, who can say how 2026 will play out? Or it might be resolved one way or another more quickly, which is what we all hope for, even if it doesn’t seem easy; and in that case, business will gradually return to normal.”
Despite variation between companies, the conflict in the Middle East has impacted sales growth by around 1 to 2 percentage points.

items.t: Luxury stocks slide – should you buy dip in the luxuries sector?
sum: Shares in luxury goods giant Hermès (PA:RMS) tanked on 15 April following warnings of a sales slowdown in its key market. But despite the luxury sector facing obvious challenges, some analysts think that there is a buying opportunity for bargain-priced luxury stocks, especially if you can spot the hidden gems.

March was a choppy month for the stock market, with the direction of travel made clear by investors’ buying trends. As the Iran war shook global outlooks, investors bought up defence and energy stocks, and went cautious in a bid to protect portfolios from volatility and profit from higher oil prices.

Hermès shares fell 8% on Wednesday, having been down more than 14% at one point in the day. The Middle East region had been the company’s fastest-growing market, but quarterly sales in the region fell 6% in constant exchange rate from the same period a year prior.

“Sales in the Middle East have, unsurprisingly, been most affected, but so too have sales in China – one of the luxury sector’s most important regions,” said Emma Wall, chief investment strategist at investment platform Hargreaves Lansdown. “Hermès also revealed sales in Paris are down, as fewer shoppers undertake international travel.”
Since the start of the conflict in Iran, Hermès shares are down 25%.

LVMH (PA:MC) – which owns the iconic Moët & Chandon, Hennessy and Louis Vuitton brands – saw its share price fall as much as 2.7% on Wednesday, though they recovered most of these losses later in the day. But LVMH shares too are down 14% since the start of the conflict.
There is clearly pressure on luxury stocks, but do the recent falls constitute a buying opportunity?

The Best Stocks to Buy Right Now for March
sum: The tech space isn't the only place to find attractive growth stocks. The consumer space is also a great place to find growth, and the sector tends to be less vulnerable to technological disruption. Let's look at two great consumer growth stocks to buy this month.

One of the best growth stories in the market right now is a little coffee shop operator out of Oregon called Dutch Bros (BROS +6.63%). While it shares Pacific Northwest roots with Starbucks, the concepts are actually quite different.

While Starbucks looks to deliver an upscale coffeehouse experience where customers can sit down, relax, and enjoy sipping their beverages, Dutch Bros is all about speed. It operates small shops that are mostly served by drive-thrus, with most not having indoor seating.

Consumers love its sugary coffee concoctions and energy drinks, and its popularity is growing as the company invests in brand awareness building. Meanwhile, the introduction of mobile buy-ahead ordering has been helping drive same-store sales, and the introduction of hot food items looks to be its next big comparable-restaurant driver.

More than anything, though, Dutch Bros is a great regional-to-national expansion story. Given the size of its coffee shops, the cost to build a new store is cheap, allowing the company to see quick returns and fund its expansion through its cash flow. It currently has fewer than 1,100 locations, with plans to open 2,029 by 2029 and 7,000 in the U.S. over the long term.
Between its same-store sales growth and expansion opportunities, Dutch Bros is a stock to own.

Two of the biggest growth drivers in the consumer space tend to be expansion for retailers and restaurants, and distribution and shelf-space gains for brands. While Dutch Bros falls into the first category, e.l.f. Beauty (ELF +2.76%) has a big opportunity in the second.

items.t: Luxury stocks slump as Middle East conflict risks one of the sector’s 'few bright spots’
sum: Luxury stocks were among the hardest hit sectors early Tuesday, with European markets heading for another day of losses as the conflict in the Middle East intensified overnight.

Shares of conglomerate LVMH, Gucci-owner Kering, and British outerwear maker Burberry were among the worst performers, with week-to-date losses approaching 10% each. The wider European blue-chip index, Stoxx 600, was down nearly 3% Tuesday, after falling 1.6% on Monday.
The Middle East has been a driver of growth in the sector, which is battling a difficult macroeconomic backdrop, and many formerly best-selling brands are struggling to resonate with consumers.
The region's strength, however, hasn't been enough to offset weakness elsewhere, notably in China, and industry giants like LVMH and Kering are still struggling to get sales back on a positive track.

"The Middle East has been one of the few bright spots," Morningstar analyst Jelena Sokolova told CNBC. "You have one area which was small, but which was very, very vibrant, and it's being affected now."

The U.S. and Israel launched widespread attacks on Iran over the weekend that killed the country's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran responded with retaliatory strikes, and the conflict now engulfs the wider Middle East region with no clear endpoint in sight.
U.S. President Donald Trump has said the war could last for four to five weeks, but that it could go on "far longer than that."

sum: French luxury goods conglomerate, LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, stock dropped more than 8% during the intraday trading session on Wednesday, 28 January 2026, after the company announced its fourth-quarter results for the calendar year ending 2025.
LVMH stock dropped 8.19% to 541 euros during Wednesday's market in France's Euronext, compared to 589.30 euros at the previous market close, according to MarketWatch data.

According to a CNBC report, LVMH's October to December quarter (Q4) results for the calendar year 2025 reportedly failed to beat investor expectations, which set a higher bar for the luxury goods conglomerate after strong earnings from competitors.

“With peers such as Richemont, Burberry, and Cucinelli reporting solid QoQ improvements and beating expectations, the bar had moved slightly higher,” Citi analysts said in a note, cited in the news portal's report.
LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE announced its October to December quarter results for the financial year ending 2025-26 on Wednesday, 28 January 2026.
LVMH reported a revenue of 80.8 billion euros in 2025, while witnessing a 1% revenue growth in the fourth quarter of the calendar year, in line with the company's third-quarter results.
The luxury goods manufacturer's profits from recurring operations in the calendar year 2025 were at 17.8 billion euros, marking a profit margin of 22%, affected by the currency fluctuations.

sum: LVMH shares slumped as much as 8.2% in early trading on Wednesday in Paris, the biggest intraday drop since April.
(Jan 28): LVMH had a poor Christmas and indicated 2026 won't get much better, dampening investors' hopes of a luxury industry rebound.

LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE, previously one of the most reliable performers in the sector, posted a worse-than-expected 3% drop in organic sales in the fourth quarter at its main fashion and leather goods unit, which includes Louis Vuitton and Christian Dior.

Three of its five divisions missed estimates in what's traditionally their strongest period, with a downbeat chief executive officer Bernard Arnault telling investors 2026 is unlikely to be straightforward, and that the group would limit spending this year as a result.
"I think we will make it through the winter," Arnault said, using gallows humour.

With the results, hopes that the luxury segment is crawling out of its post-pandemic slump have been dashed. With cost-of-living pressures, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty weighing on spending, companies in the sector are struggling to bounce back. Brands have also suffered from a consumer backlash after steep price increases.

"The journey back to growth for the sector, and LVMH as its proxy, will remain bumpy in the coming quarters, highly dependent on the external backdrop," JPMorgan analyst Chiara Battistini said in a note.
